facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Reported leverage rose and then fell with earnings, not with borrowing. Net debt was 3.73x reported EBITDA at the end of fiscal 2024, 5.89x at the end of fiscal 2025 and 6.24x at January 2, 2026, then 5.04x and 4.62x at the next two quarter ends. facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Revenue durability is strong in structure but weakening in practice. Recurring rental is 95% of revenue and the 10 largest customers are under 10%, yet revenue fell 2.53% in fiscal 2025, or 4.37% without the extra week, mostly because lost business exceeded new business, and fell 1.90% in the nine months to July 3, 2026, with net volumes down 4.5% in the third quarter. Creditors are exposed to customer retention, not to end-market demand. facts.label: Transaction summary and new debt issues

facts.text: Revenue durability is the weakest operating dimension. facts.text: Vestis rents and services uniforms and sells workplace supplies, including restroom and first-aid products, mats, towels and linens, to a very large number of small and large customers in the United States and Canada, with Canada 8.98% of revenue. facts.label: Revenue drivers and pricing power
facts.text: Revenue is recurring and weakly cyclical but is being lost account by account. Uniforms revenue fell 7.57% in fiscal 2025 while workplace supplies rose 0.89%, rental revenue fell mainly because lost business exceeded new business, and direct sales fell with the loss of a national account. Net volumes fell 4.5% in the third quarter of 2026 and pricing offset part of it, but pricing power is contested: a shareholder class action alleges misleading statements about pricing practices, so price-led recovery carries legal and retention risk. facts.label: Competitive forces
facts.text: Rivalry is intense and local: the industry is fragmented, two competitors of size are named, and many customers could run the service in-house. Buyer power is moderate because customers sign multi-year contracts with exit costs but can challenge pricing and contracts, supplier power is concentrated in single-supplier inputs and two plants in Mexico that make about 60% of uniforms and linens, and entry is limited by route density and scale. In-house operation is the main substitute. The result is price pressure that caps margin recovery and increases the importance of retention. Basis: 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, pages 11–14; Business & governance (CP-1A)

facts.label: Downside scenario
facts.text: The initiating condition is account losses that continue after the targeted volume exits end, with plan savings arriving late. The first operational break is revenue falling faster than costs, so reported EBITDA stalls near its last twelve months level and cash interest, which takes 38.00% of EBITDA, stops falling; free cash flow after finance lease principal, 44.61% of EBITDA, would shrink toward the negative level of fiscal 2025. The financial transmission is leverage that stays near 4.62x while the covenant maximum falls to 4.75x and then 4.50x, with each 1% rise in rates cutting cover to 2.33x. facts.label: Overall credit view
facts.text: Overall, Vestis presents an adequate business profile supported by scale, recurring weekly route revenue, low customer concentration and ample undrawn liquidity, but credit quality is constrained by 4.62x leverage, thin cover, falling revenue and claims outside term debt. Cash-flow durability appears adequate because free cash flow has recovered, but part of the recovery is working capital and lease financing. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on renewal of the receivables facility before August 2027 and on leverage staying below the falling covenant maximums. The primary downside path is customer loss with delayed savings. Further analysis would require the credit agreement, fiscal fourth-quarter results and a peer or market reference. The top risk is continued revenue erosion. ## Findings
### Bottom line

The seven supplied documents are ready, with limitations, for the credit snapshot's financial, business and fundamental credit work through the quarter ended July 3, 2026, but nothing reaches the fiscal year-end or the 2026-11-05 as-of date.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, pages 1, 20; EX-99.1_2026-08-11_vstsq3fy26earningsrelease-.htm.jsonl, page 1; calculation C2

Every reported covenant, liquidity and leverage position therefore dates from July 3, 2026 at the latest, which is 125 days before the as-of date. The fiscal quarter ending October 2, 2026, whose maximum net leverage covenant is 4.75x, is not covered. The executed credit agreement, the proxy statement and any credit rating are also missing, so covenant definitions, directors and owners remain open questions.

## Findings
### Bottom line

Leverage has fallen from its January 2, 2026 peak but remains high: net debt was 4.62x reported EBITDA and cash interest cover only 2.63x for the twelve months to July 3, 2026, so creditors still depend on the earnings recovery holding.
Basis: calculation N5; calculation LE3; calculation LI3

The improvement comes from reported EBITDA rising 16.58% above its fiscal 2025 level while principal fell to USD 1,097.5 million, not from any change in the debt stack, which is entirely floating-rate senior secured term debt. Net debt here leaves out finance leases and receivables sold, and the issuer's own leverage measure of 4.10x uses a different EBITDA and a wider definition.
Basis: calculation G3; calculation B3; 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, pages 19–21; EX-99.1_2026-08-11_vstsq3fy26earningsrelease-.htm.jsonl, page 16
### Key findings

Reported leverage rose and then fell with earnings, not with borrowing. Net debt was 3.73x reported EBITDA at the end of fiscal 2024, 5.89x at the end of fiscal 2025 and 6.24x at January 2, 2026, then 5.04x and 4.62x at the next two quarter ends. Reported EBITDA fell 36.21% in fiscal 2025 while debt at carrying value rose 0.65%, so the ratio worsened with almost no net new borrowing; net debt has since fallen 8.61% from the fiscal 2025 year-end through repayments funded by operating cash flow, and the recovery in twelve-month EBITDA has done the rest.
Basis: calculation G1; calculation G2; calculation G4; calculation N1; calculation N2; calculation N3; calculation N4; calculation N5

Cash interest cover shows the same shape: 3.09x in fiscal 2024, 2.04x in fiscal 2025, 1.96x at January 2, 2026 and 2.63x at July 3, 2026. Cash interest paid on principal debt fell 9.62% to USD 84.6 million over the last twelve months, helped by repayments and a weighted-average term loan rate of 6.23% for nine months against 6.80% a year earlier, but cover remains well under three times, so a renewed earnings fall would erode it quickly. Interest paid on finance leases and the securitization fees sit outside this figure, which flatters cover.
Basis: calculation G6; calculation LI3; 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, pages 16, 21; EX-99.1_2026-08-11_vstsq3fy26earningsrelease-.htm.jsonl, page 14

Cash generation improved by far more than earnings. Free cash flow, meaning operating cash flow less purchases of property and equipment, equalled 61.27% of reported EBITDA over the last twelve months against 3.02% in fiscal 2025. Part of the swing is working capital: receivables, inventories and rental merchandise released cash and the receivables sale facility was used more heavily, so the improvement is not all repeatable.
Basis: calculation LF3; calculation F2; 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, pages 8, 50–51

Liquidity, cash plus the undrawn revolver, rose at each of the three 2026 quarter ends and was 18.09% higher at July 3, 2026 than at fiscal 2025 year-end. The revolver was undrawn at both April 3 and July 3, 2026, but the USD 250 million receivables facility, which is off balance sheet, is scheduled to end on August 2, 2027, inside twelve months of the as-of date, and no renewal or replacement is stated in the sources read.
Basis: calculation G8; calculation Q2; calculation Q3; calculation Q4; calculation Q5; 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, page 37

The debt is concentrated and floating-rate. USD 436 million of Term Loan A-2 falls due in fiscal 2028, with the undrawn revolver, and USD 661.5 million of Term Loan B-1 in fiscal 2031, so the first debt maturity is fiscal 2028, where Term Loan A-2 alone is 1.96x reported EBITDA against 4.93x for all principal. The annual report's maturity table shows no scheduled principal before fiscal 2028, while the latest quarterly report still describes quarterly amortization on Term Loan B-1; the two statements are not reconciled.
Basis: calculation S2; calculation S3; 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, pages 113, 116; 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, pages 19–20

Definitions matter as much as the trend. Net debt here is carrying-value debt less cash, so it omits finance leases, letters of credit and receivables sold under the securitization facility. The issuer's Net Debt adds finance leases and letters of credit to principal debt and divides by a covenant-adjusted EBITDA higher than reported EBITDA, giving 4.10x against 4.62x here, yet neither figure includes the USD 212.3 million of receivables sold at July 3, 2026, up from USD 202.5 million at October 3, 2025, although the credit agreement's debt definition counts advances under a receivables facility. Whether those advances equal the sold balance is not established without the credit agreement.
Basis: calculation B1; calculation B2; calculation B3; calculation G10; 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, pages 37, 52; EX-99.1_2026-08-11_vstsq3fy26earningsrelease-.htm.jsonl, pages 10, 16

No event after July 3, 2026 that changes net debt is stated in the sources. The transformation plan that the annual report describes as a subsequent event was approved in the first quarter of fiscal 2026, before this balance sheet, so it is already in the 2026 figures and was kept out of fiscal 2025. Fiscal 2025 adjusted EBITDA is stated two ways, in the release reconciliation and as USD 272.6 million in the outlook table, and the releases do not explain the difference; this analysis uses the reconciliation figure because it carries the add-backs.
Basis: 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, page 147; EX-99.1_2026-08-11_vstsq3fy26earningsrelease-.htm.jsonl, pages 4, 14; calculation G12
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest case that credit quality is better than 4.62x suggests rests on the issuer's own measures: adjusted EBITDA for the last twelve months was 30.46% above reported EBITDA, net debt over adjusted EBITDA was 3.54x, and the issuer reports 4.10x on its covenant basis. It would win if the severance, transformation and separation add-backs prove one-off and the savings plan delivers, because adjusted EBITDA would then track cash earnings.
Basis: calculation G11; calculation A1; calculation B3

The opposite case is that the ratio flatters. The twelve-month window contains the 14-week fourth quarter of fiscal 2025, working capital released cash, and finance leases and receivable sales sit outside net debt while the securitization fees are a recurring funding cost that the issuer adds back. It would win if fiscal fourth-quarter 2026 reported EBITDA fails to hold the recent level, which the covenant ceiling of 4.75x for the quarter ending October 2, 2026 and 4.50x after would then test; the issuer reports 4.10x at July 3, 2026 against a 5.00x maximum, and headroom cannot be judged without the credit agreement.
Basis: calculation A1; calculation Y3; 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, pages 20, 37; EX-99.1_2026-08-11_vstsq3fy26earningsrelease-.htm.jsonl, page 16
### Limitations

Reported EBITDA is calculated because the issuer states none, and adjusted EBITDA, net debt and the leverage ratio the issuer prints appear only in the unaudited earnings releases; fiscal 2024 adjusted EBITDA is not supplied. Interest paid is stated only to USD 0.1 million and only for principal debt.
Basis: EX-99.1_2026-08-11_vstsq3fy26earningsrelease-.htm.jsonl, pages 14, 16; 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, page 113

The balance sheet series has five dates and no prior-year interim balance sheet is supplied, so year-on-year leverage can be compared only at fiscal year-ends; fiscal 2025 has 53 weeks and every twelve-month figure to July 3, 2026 spans 53 weeks. The credit agreement is not supplied, so covenant definitions and headroom are the issuer's statements only.
Basis: 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, page 65; 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, pages 6, 20; calculation Y4; calculation Y5; calculation Y6

## Gaps

- High: the issuer states fiscal 2025 adjusted EBITDA two ways, in the release reconciliation and as USD 272.6 million in the outlook table, and fiscal 2024 and fiscal 2023 adjusted EBITDA are not supplied. Adjusted leverage and cover are therefore available for fiscal 2025 and the twelve-month windows only, and the fiscal 2025 figure depends on which statement is right. Closing it needs the issuer's fourth-quarter fiscal 2025 release or an explanation of the difference.
Basis: EX-99.1_2026-08-11_vstsq3fy26earningsrelease-.htm.jsonl, pages 4, 14; calculation G12

- High: the credit agreement is not supplied, so the covenant definitions, the receivables facility treatment and the ranking among the facilities rest on the issuer's summaries. This restricts any covenant headroom or ranking conclusion; no covenant capacity is inferred here. Closing it needs the executed credit agreement and its two amendments.

- High: net debt on the issuer's definition and the covenant definition differs from carrying-value net debt by USD 176.907 million at July 3, 2026, and the receivables sold under the securitization facility are in neither measure. The issuer's net leverage of 4.10x and the 4.62x here are not comparable without the credit agreement. Closing it needs the agreement's definition of advances under a receivables facility.
Basis: EX-99.1_2026-08-11_vstsq3fy26earningsrelease-.htm.jsonl, pages 10, 16; 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, pages 37, 52; calculation B2

- Medium: the income statement presents no gross profit because cost of services excludes depreciation and amortization, so gross profit is not calculated. Closing it would need an issuer gross profit definition.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, page 5

- Medium: where a source prints a dash the cell is marked not supplied rather than zero. This affects the loss or gain on sale of an equity investment in most periods, several borrowing, dividend and investing lines in the cash flow columns, and the loss on extinguishment of debt; the amounts are nil or not applicable on the face of the statements, but the method treats a dash as missing. No action is needed beyond reading each as nil.

- Medium: the third-quarter report presents non-cash lease expense and changes in lease liabilities as separate cash flow lines for nine months 2026 and 2025, while earlier filings do not, so those two lines are marked not presented for the other columns. Operating cash flow totals are unchanged. Closing it needs the earlier filings restated on the new presentation.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, page 8; 10-Q_2026-04-03_vsts-20260403.htm.jsonl, page 7

- Medium: interest paid is stated only to USD 0.1 million and only for principal debt. Finance lease interest and securitization fees are outside it, so cash interest cover is overstated against total cash financing cost, and fiscal 2024 interest paid is given only for the full year. Closing it needs interest paid including leases and fees by quarter.

- Medium: the quarterly reports carry a balance sheet only against the fiscal 2025 year-end, so no prior-year interim leverage can be built and the leverage series has five dates. No fiscal 2023 balance sheet is supplied, so fiscal 2023 leverage is not calculable, and the fiscal 2023 statements are consolidated and combined before the separation. Closing it needs the prior-year interim balance sheets and the fiscal 2023 balance sheet.

- Medium: every twelve-month figure to the 2026 quarter ends includes the 14-week fourth quarter of fiscal 2025 and spans 53 weeks, so ratios at those dates are not on a 52-week basis; the first 52-week window ends with the fiscal 2026 fourth quarter, which is not supplied. Closing it needs the fiscal 2026 fourth-quarter report.
Basis: 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, page 65; EX-99.1_2026-08-11_vstsq3fy26earningsrelease-.htm.jsonl, page 14; calculation Y4; calculation Y5; calculation Y6

- Medium: the maturity ladder is drawn at July 3, 2026 from each tranche's stated maturity because the quarterly report prints none, and the sources disagree on whether Term Loan B-1 still has scheduled quarterly amortization. Years with no maturity are left out instead of shown as zero. Closing it needs the credit agreement's repayment schedule.

- Medium: the filings call all three credit-agreement facilities senior secured but state no ranking among them; the debt stack treats them as equal rank, which is a reading and not a stated fact, and the revolver's borrowing margin and rate type are not stated. Closing it needs the executed credit agreement.

- Medium: the securitization fees the issuer adds back differ from the fees in the notes, with USD 13.555 million against USD 13.0 million for fiscal 2025 and USD 8.668 million against USD 8.4 million for nine months 2026. The releases do not say what the difference contains. Closing it needs the issuer's reconciliation of the fees.

Basis: EX-99.1_2026-08-11_vstsq3fy26earningsrelease-.htm.jsonl, page 14; 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, page 147; 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, page 37; calculation G14; calculation G15

- Medium: the first-quarter 2025 adjusted EBITDA is 81.201 in the first-quarter release but implied at 81.145 by the second-quarter release, and the issuer-stated fiscal 2025 free cash flow of 5.9 differs from the statement-derived 5.769; both differences are small and unexplained. Closing it needs the issuer's explanation of the restated figure.

Basis: EX-99.1_2026-02-10_vstsq1fy26earningsrelease-.htm.jsonl, page 12; EX-99.1_2026-05-12_vstsq2fy26earningsrelease-.htm.jsonl, page 14; EX-99.1_2026-08-11_vstsq3fy26earningsrelease-.htm.jsonl, page 4; calculation G13; calculation G16

- Medium: the revolver availability at September 27, 2024 is not stated, so liquidity for fiscal 2024 is not supplied, and the sources give no maintenance and growth split of capital expenditure, so only total capital expenditure is carried. Closing it needs the issuer's capital expenditure split.

- Medium: the substitute insurance collateral facility of about USD 24.8 million, a contingent arrangement entered in the first quarter of fiscal 2026 that replaces bank and surety-backed letters of credit, is not funded debt and is not in any ratio; its fees are amortized to interest expense. Closing it needs the facility terms.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-01-02_vsts-20260102.htm.jsonl, page 26

- Low: the revenue and EBITDA chart omits the 14-week fourth quarter of fiscal 2025 to keep one duration per row; its reported revenue and adjusted EBITDA are stated in the basis cell. No action is needed.
Basis: EX-99.1_2026-08-11_vstsq3fy26earningsrelease-.htm.jsonl, page 14

- Low: no event after July 3, 2026 that changes net debt is stated in the supplied sources, so the post-balance-sheet table records none; the sources are not dated after August 11, 2026, so later events are not established. Closing it needs the fiscal 2026 fourth-quarter report.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, page 56; EX-99.1_2026-08-11_vstsq3fy26earningsrelease-.htm.jsonl, page 1

spans.text: ## Request

Vestis Corp (issuer id vsts), as of 2026-11-05, credit snapshot pathway. Scope: the business, ownership, governance, litigation and capital allocation facts in the seven supplied annual, quarterly and earnings-release documents, translated into creditor consequences, using the supplied Source readiness findings.
## Sources

## Findings
### Bottom line

Vestis presents medium governance and business risk for creditors: the supplied documents identify no sponsor or controlling holder and revenue is very diversified, but customer losses, executive turnover, shareholder litigation and a rising restructuring cost estimate show execution risk.

The main protection against value leakage is contractual, not governance: since May 2025 the credit agreement restricts dividends and share repurchases, and no dividend has been paid since the first half of fiscal 2025, but the restriction can end after the quarter ending October 2, 2026 once covenants are met, before leverage reaches 4.50x. The restructuring plan is the key test: its cost estimate rose from a range of USD 25 million to USD 30 million to a range of USD 35 million to USD 40 million, with USD 31.2 million already recognized.
Basis: 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, pages 59, 67; 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, pages 17, 20, 42; calculation P3; calculation P6
### Key findings

Revenue durability is strong in structure but weakening in practice. Recurring rental is 95% of revenue and the 10 largest customers are under 10%, yet revenue fell 2.53% in fiscal 2025, or 4.37% without the extra week, mostly because lost business exceeded new business, and fell 1.90% in the nine months to July 3, 2026, with net volumes down 4.5% in the third quarter. Creditors are exposed to customer retention, not to end-market demand.
Basis: 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, pages 10, 11, 68; 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, page 44; calculation R1; calculation R2; calculation S10

Operating profit is thin and is recovering through cost action, not growth. The fiscal 2025 operating margin was 2.36%, and the United States segment margin fell from 11.79% in fiscal 2023 to 6.19% in fiscal 2025 before recovering to 9.24% in the third quarter of 2026 from 6.63% a year earlier, while uniforms revenue fell 7.57% in fiscal 2025 and workplace supplies revenue rose 0.89%.

Basis: 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, pages 89, 118, 132; 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, pages 21, 33, 34; calculation D7; calculation S2; calculation S4; calculation S6; calculation S7; calculation R6; calculation R7

No sponsor or controlling holder is identified, which removes the usual extraction channel but also any identified source of equity support. The shares were distributed to Aramark stockholders in September 2023, holders of record are in the hundreds, and a letter agreement with Corvex Management LP and a director, amended in May 2025, is known only by its title.

Distribution risk is low today because the lenders hold a lock, but the lock is time-limited. Dividends paid in fiscal 2025 were 239.21% of free cash flow, none has been paid since, and the May 2025 amendment restricts dividends and repurchases until the earlier of a compliant quarter after October 2, 2026 or two consecutive quarters at 4.50x or lower, so the first test needs covenant compliance but not lower leverage.
Basis: 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, pages 59, 91, 143; 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, pages 20, 38; calculation F2

Management continuity is a weakness that the cost plan depends on. Four executive separation agreements are dated in 2025, fiscal 2025 severance rose USD 13.9 million, and the three quarterly reports since the annual report are signed by an interim chief financial officer, whose offer letters are dated December 15, 2025 and June 12, 2026; no permanent appointment is stated, the documents give no reasons for the departures, and no individual is assessed.

The restructuring plan costs more than first stated and has not yet been shown to pay. The estimate midpoint rose 36.36% from the annual report to the third-quarter report, consulting recognized of USD 23.2 million already exceeds the latest consulting estimate by USD 8.2 million, and USD 31.2 million, 78.00% of the high end, has been recognized in nine months. Management says about USD 30 million of an expected USD 50 million in-year benefit, 60.00%, is realized, which is its own claim.

Basis: 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, page 67; 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, pages 17, 42; EX-99.1_2026-08-11_vstsq3fy26earningsrelease-.htm.jsonl, page 2; calculation P4; calculation P5; calculation P6; calculation P7

Shareholder litigation is an unquantified contingent claim ahead of equity. Two securities class actions are pending, in Georgia and New York, with a Delaware bylaw challenge and derivative suits; the Georgia motion to dismiss was denied on September 30, 2025, the New York motion was granted in part and denied in part on July 31, 2026, and a class certification motion was filed in Georgia on April 10, 2026. The company says it cannot predict outcomes and gives no loss estimate.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, pages 28–32

Labor and pension costs are structural. About 59.23% of employees are union-represented under a large number of collective bargaining agreements, multiemployer plan contributions rose 10.68% from fiscal 2023 to fiscal 2025, and some plans are in critical status, so a withdrawal could become a debt-like claim. Finance leases, operating leases and insurance reserves are further claims outside term debt.
Basis: 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, pages 17, 32, 123; 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, pages 6, 15; calculation L1; calculation D2; calculation Z1; calculation Z2; calculation Z3

Creditor recourse rests on guarantees and liens from wholly owned domestic material subsidiaries, so the Canadian business, 8.98% of revenue and 5.49% of segment operating income, may sit outside the package; this is not established because the subsidiary list is not supplied.
Basis: 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, pages 72, 155; calculation M8; calculation R8
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest case for lower risk is that nothing in the documents shows value extraction or creditor-adverse conduct: there is no sponsor, no acquisition debt, no priming or exchange transaction, the annual audit was unqualified and internal control effective, the revolver was undrawn with USD 294.2 million available, covenants were met at July 3, 2026 and the United States segment margin has recovered to 9.24%. It would win if the class action is dismissed or settled within insurance, finance leadership is made permanent, and the plan delivers its savings at or below the current estimate.
Basis: 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, pages 84, 87, 148; 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, pages 20–21; calculation F7; calculation S6

The strongest case for higher risk is that the lock lifts before leverage is low and the plan overruns. Risk would move to high if the plan estimate rises again, if consulting keeps outrunning its estimate, if class certification is granted without insurance cover, if another executive departure or a large customer loss follows, or if dividends or repurchases resume while leverage is above 4.50x. The proxy statement or the letter agreement could move the view either way by showing who controls votes and board seats.
Basis: 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, page 59; 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, page 29; calculation P5
### Limitations

- The proxy statement is not supplied, so board independence, committee roles, pay and beneficial ownership are not established; the medium rating rests on exhibits and signatures and could move either way if the proxy shows an anchor holder or weak independence.

- The letter agreement with Corvex Management LP is known only by its title, so whether it carries board, voting or standstill rights is not established; the finding that no holder is identified as controlling depends on it.
Basis: 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, page 154

- The distribution lock is known from the issuer's summaries of the May 2025 amendment, not from the amendment, so exceptions or baskets that would permit dividends are not established; the finding that leakage risk is low now rests on that summary.

- No loss estimate, accrual or insurance recovery is stated for the shareholder suits, so the exposure cannot be sized; the view that it is a contingent rather than near-term cash claim could be wrong.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, pages 28–32
- Nothing after August 11, 2026 is supplied, so executive changes, rulings and plan costs since then are not established and the turnover and plan findings may be out of date at the as-of date.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, page 56; Source readiness (CP-0)
- The seven documents contain no sponsor, rating agency or investor presentation material, so sponsor willingness and market perception are not assessed and are not inferred.
Basis: 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, page 62
### Company and operating model
| Item | Fact | Credit relevance | Source |

| What the company does | Rents and services uniforms and supplies workplace products (restroom supplies, first-aid and safety products, floor mats, towels, linens), delivered by route on a weekly cycle under multi-year contracts | Weekly route service and exit costs on early termination give recurring, contracted cash flow that is the base for debt service | 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, pages 10–12 |

| Revenue model | Recurring rental 95% of fiscal 2025 revenue; direct sales of customized uniforms 5% | Direct sales are the volatile part: the fiscal 2025 loss of a national account cut direct sales revenue by USD 15.6 million | 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, page 68 |

| Scale and concentration | Over 325 sites, over 3,300 routes and over 300,000 customer accounts; the 10 largest customers are under 10% of revenue (calculation E1) | No single customer decides coverage, but losses of whole accounts still moved fiscal 2025 revenue | 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, pages 11, 13; 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, page 68 |

| Geography | United States 91.02% and Canada 8.98% of fiscal 2025 revenue | Canada is small; whether Canadian subsidiaries guarantee the credit facilities is not established | 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, page 118; 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, page 72 |

| Product mix | Uniforms 38.34% and workplace supplies 61.66% of fiscal 2025 revenue; uniforms were 41.35% in fiscal 2023 and 37.10% in the nine months to July 3, 2026 | Mix is moving to workplace supplies; margin by product line is not disclosed, so the effect on profit is not established | 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, page 118; 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, page 21 |

| Customer retention | Fiscal 2025 rental revenue fell USD 89.0 million, of which USD 69.9 million was lost business in excess of new business (78.54%) | Retention, not end-market demand, is the main revenue driver; the issuer discloses no retention rate | 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, page 68 |

| Cost structure | Fiscal 2025 cost of services 73.50% of revenue, selling, general and administrative 18.92% and depreciation and amortization 5.23% | High fixed route, plant and labor costs make margin sensitive to volume loss | 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, pages 15, 89 |

| Operating margin | Fiscal 2025 operating income USD 64.4 million, 2.36% of revenue; United States segment margin 6.19% in fiscal 2025 against 11.79% in fiscal 2023 | Thin consolidated margin leaves little cushion for interest and Plan costs | 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, page 89; 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, pages 118, 132 |

| Sourcing and manufacturing | About 60% of uniforms and linens are made in two plants in Mexico; certain raw materials and products come from a single supplier | Tariff, trade or supplier disruption would hit unit cost directly | 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, page 13 |

| Workforce | About 59.23% of employees are represented by unions, under over 200 collective bargaining agreements | Wage settlements and multiemployer pension contributions are quasi-fixed charges ahead of debt service | 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, pages 17, 32 |
### Company profile

### Transaction summary and new debt issues

Vestis was created by a spin-off, not a sponsor transaction. Aramark distributed the shares to its stockholders on September 30, 2023, and the company paid about USD 1,457 million in cash to Aramark at the separation, the day the senior secured credit agreement was signed; the documents do not itemise the funding.

No new term loan tranche has been added since the first refinancing. Term Loan A-1 was refinanced in February 2024 with a USD 800 million Term Loan B-1 due February 2031, a USD 250 million receivables securitization facility was added in August 2024 and its proceeds repaid term loans, and the May 2025 amendment raised the covenant ceiling to 5.25x while restricting dividends, repurchases and receivables facilities.

Other transactions were small. A 39% equity interest in a Japanese uniform company was sold for USD 36.8 million in October 2024 with the proceeds applied to debt, a substitute insurance collateral facility of about USD 24.8 million replaced bank and surety letters of credit, and no significant acquisitions were made in fiscal 2023, 2024 or 2025.

### T2D.9 Risk level register
| Risk-Level Driver | Evidence | Risk Mechanic | Credit Implication | Evidence Quality | Source Trace | Countervailing Evidence | Limitation |

| No identified sponsor or controlling holder | Shares were distributed to Aramark stockholders; about 739 holders of record; no sponsor, fund or equity cure is described | Without a sponsor there is no documented distribution or recapitalization pattern, and also no identified source of fresh equity | Lowers extraction risk; leaves creditors to rely on operating cash flow | Medium | 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, pages 59, 145 | A letter agreement with Corvex Management LP and a director exists, and beneficial ownership is not supplied | Proxy statement and agreement not supplied |

| Distribution policy and covenant lock | Dividends paid USD 13.8 million in fiscal 2025, above free cash flow; none since the May 2025 amendment, which restricts dividends and repurchases | Distributions can return after 2026-10-02 once covenants are met, before leverage reaches 4.50x | Lowers risk now; raises it from the first compliant quarter after 2026-10-02 | High | 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, pages 59, 91, 143; 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, pages 20, 38 | The second test requires 4.50x or lower for two consecutive quarters | Exceptions and baskets not supplied |

| Executive turnover and interim finance leadership | Four executive separation agreements in 2025; interim chief financial officer for three reported quarters; fiscal 2025 severance up USD 13.9 million | Turnover during a customer-loss year and a cost plan raises execution and reporting risk | Raises the chance the Plan misses its cash and savings targets | High | 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, pages 68, 154, 155; 10-Q_2026-01-02_vsts-20260102.htm.jsonl, page 52; 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, page 56 | New executive agreements were signed in 2025; the annual audit was unqualified and internal control was effective | Reasons for departures not stated |

| Transformation Plan cost path | Cost estimate USD 25 million to USD 30 million rose to USD 35 million to USD 40 million; USD 31.2 million recognized in nine months; savings of at least USD 75 million claimed | Spending leads and savings lag, so near-term free cash flow carries the cost | Raises refinancing risk if savings arrive late | High | 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, page 67; 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, pages 17, 42; EX-99.1_2026-08-11_vstsq3fy26earningsrelease-.htm.jsonl, page 2 | Management reports about USD 30 million of the USD 50 million in-year benefit already realized (60.00%, calculation P4) | Savings baseline not disclosed |

| Open shareholder litigation | Two securities class actions, a Delaware bylaw action and derivative actions; the Georgia motion to dismiss was denied on 2025-09-30 and class certification is pending | Damages, defense cost and indemnification of directors and officers are contingent cash claims with no estimate | Contingent claim ahead of equity; size unknown | Medium | 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, pages 28–31 | The company states most other legal matters are not expected to be material and intends to defend vigorously | No loss estimate, accrual or insurance recovery stated |

| Labor and pension exposure | About 59.23% of employees are union-represented under over 200 agreements; three of the four named multiemployer pension plans are in critical or critical and declining status; contributions rose 10.68% from fiscal 2023 to fiscal 2025 | Wage settlements and contributions are quasi-fixed; a plan withdrawal would crystallize liability | Pressures margin and could add a debt-like claim | Medium | 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, pages 17, 32, 123 | No surcharge is imposed on contributions to the four named plans; the agreement covering most participants of one fund expires 2026-05-22 and its outcome is not stated | Outcome of that agreement and withdrawal liability amounts not supplied |
Sponsor / Governance Risk Level: Medium

The risk level is driven by dispersed ownership with a time-limited distribution lock and a rising plan cost, because creditors have no sponsor to extract value but also none to support execution, which implies medium risk for creditors. Countervailing evidence is the unqualified audit, effective internal control and the recovery of the United States segment margin. Further analysis requires the proxy statement, the credit agreement and any loss estimate for the shareholder suits.

## Findings
### Bottom line

Vestis is an adequate but fragile credit: recurring route revenue and recovering cash flow support debt service, but 4.62x leverage, thin margins and falling revenue leave little room if cost savings or the receivables facility renewal disappoint.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation L1; calculation L6; calculation F1

Deleveraging is real but recent: reported net debt to EBITDA fell from 5.89x at the fiscal 2025 year end to 4.62x at July 3, 2026, and free cash flow reached 61.27% of reported EBITDA over twelve months. Two dates matter more than the trend: the covenant maximum falls to 4.75x for the quarter ending October 2, 2026, and the USD 250 million receivables facility ends on August 2, 2027.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, pages 20, 37; Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation L1; calculation L2; calculation F1
### Key findings

Leverage has fallen but is still the main constraint. Reported net debt was 4.62x EBITDA at July 3, 2026 against 5.89x at the fiscal 2025 year end and a 6.24x peak at January 2, 2026, and cash interest cover was 2.63x, with 38.00% of EBITDA paid as cash interest. The issuer's own ratio is 4.10x, on a wider debt definition and a higher EBITDA, while counting finance leases and receivables sold gives 6.29x reported EBITDA and 4.82x adjusted EBITDA, so the improvement is real but the base is thin.

Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); EX-99.1_2026-08-11_vstsq3fy26earningsrelease-.htm.jsonl, page 16; 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, pages 6, 37; calculation L1; calculation L2; calculation L3; calculation L6; calculation L11; calculation L14; calculation L16; calculation L17

Cash conversion has improved sharply, but part of the improvement will not repeat. Free cash flow was 61.27% of reported EBITDA over the last twelve months against 3.02% in fiscal 2025, helped by working capital that released cash and by a larger sale of receivables, and fiscal 2024 was inflated by the one-time inflow when the receivables facility started. After finance lease principal, free cash flow was 44.61% of reported EBITDA over twelve months and negative in fiscal 2025, which shows how much lease financing flatters the headline figure.

Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, pages 73, 91; 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, pages 8, 50; calculation F1; calculation F2; calculation F4; calculation F5; calculation F6; calculation F7

Revenue durability is the weakest operating dimension. Revenue fell 2.53% in fiscal 2025, or 4.37% without the extra week, and 1.90% in the nine months to July 3, 2026, mainly because lost business exceeded new business, and net volumes fell 4.5% in the third quarter, partly by choice under the cost plan. Recurring rental is 95% of revenue and the largest customers are small, so the risk is steady account loss, not one concentrated customer.

Basis: 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, pages 10, 11, 68; 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, page 44; Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation R4; calculation R5; calculation R6; calculation R13

Margins are thin but recovering through cost action. Reported EBITDA margin was 10.67% in fiscal 2024, 6.98% in fiscal 2025 and 8.26% over the last twelve months, and the United States segment margin was 9.24% in the third quarter of 2026 against 6.63% a year earlier. Part of the recovery is the absence of the fiscal 2025 bad debt and severance charges, so the margin gain is not all new.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, page 68; calculation R1; calculation R2; calculation R3; calculation R8; calculation R9

Liquidity is ample and no term debt matures before fiscal 2028, but one refinancing comes earlier. Liquidity rose 18.09% from the fiscal 2025 year end, the revolver is undrawn, and Term Loan A-2 and the revolver mature in September 2028, but the receivables facility ends on August 2, 2027 and funds 19.34% of principal debt in sold receivables. Funding that balance on the revolver would cut liquidity by 60.34% and lift net debt to 5.57x reported EBITDA.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, pages 20, 37; calculation Q2; calculation Q3; calculation Q6; calculation Q7; calculation Q8

The covenant path tightens just as the distribution lock can lift. The maximum net leverage falls from 5.00x to 4.75x for the quarter ending October 2, 2026 and to 4.50x afterwards, against an issuer ratio of 4.10x, and the lock on dividends and share repurchases ends on the earlier of a compliant quarter after October 2, 2026 or two quarters at 4.50x or lower. Covenant headroom is not calculated here because the credit agreement is not supplied; Legal & covenants and Covenant capacity own that test.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, page 20; 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, page 59; EX-99.1_2026-08-11_vstsq3fy26earningsrelease-.htm.jsonl, page 16; calculation L11

Financial policy is creditor-protective for now. No sponsor or controlling holder is identified, dividends paid in fiscal 2025 were 239.21% of free cash flow before the lock, and none has been paid since, but executive turnover, shareholder litigation with no loss estimate and a plan whose cost estimate rose 36.36% add execution risk around the covenant step-downs.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation F11; calculation P1; calculation P2; calculation P3

The primary downside path is continued customer loss with delayed savings, followed by the covenant step-down and the 2027 receivables renewal arriving together. A 1% rise in interest rates on the floating-rate term loans would cut cash interest cover from 2.63x to 2.33x on unchanged EBITDA, and no interest rate hedge is described in the sources read.
Basis: 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, pages 43, 83; Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation S1; calculation S2
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest case for a stronger credit is the earnings and cash trend: adjusted EBITDA is 30.46% above reported EBITDA over the last twelve months, the issuer reports 4.10x, its fiscal 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance of USD 310.0 million to USD 315.0 million is 7.60% above the last twelve months at its midpoint, and it raised its free cash flow guidance to USD 160.0 million to USD 170.0 million. It would win if fourth-quarter adjusted EBITDA reaches the implied USD 84.0 million to USD 89.0 million, revenue stabilizes once the targeted volume exits end, and the receivables facility is renewed, because leverage would keep falling through the covenant step-downs.
Basis: EX-99.1_2026-08-11_vstsq3fy26earningsrelease-.htm.jsonl, pages 4, 16; Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation L11; calculation L13; calculation G1; calculation G2; calculation G3

The strongest case for a weaker credit is that the recovery leans on working capital, add-backs and lease financing. Adjusted EBITDA includes transformation, severance and securitization add-backs, finance leases and sold receivables sit outside the issuer's net debt, and revenue is still falling. It would win if revenue keeps declining after the exits end, the plan estimate rises again, or the receivables facility is renewed only on worse terms, because cover near 2.00x and a 4.50x maximum would then be tested together.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, pages 44, 50; calculation L13; calculation L16; calculation L17; calculation F4; calculation R6
### Limitations

- The fiscal fourth quarter ended October 2, 2026 is not reported in any supplied document, so the finding that leverage keeps falling toward the next covenant step-down cannot be tested against the first test after the latest accounts.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, page 20; calculation B4

- The credit agreement is not supplied, so every covenant conclusion rests on the stated maximums and the issuer's ratio and is directional; it is not a headroom or capacity finding, and the debt in each definition cannot be reconciled.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, pages 20, 52

- The all-in leverage figures add finance leases and sold receivables to net debt and are analyst calculations, not issuer measures; they change the finding on how thin the base is, and reported EBITDA is already after securitization fees.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation L15; calculation L16; calculation L17

- No rating, peer data or current market price is supplied, so scale, margin and market access are judged against the issuer's own history, not against peers or current market conditions; the assessment of refinancing access cannot be tested.
Basis: Source readiness (CP-0)
- The fiscal 2026 outlook is management guidance on issuer definitions and is not independently verified; the finding that cash generation holds through the fourth quarter depends on it.
Basis: EX-99.1_2026-08-11_vstsq3fy26earningsrelease-.htm.jsonl, page 4
### Strengths and weaknesses

The main credit strengths are undrawn liquidity with no term maturity before fiscal 2028, which covers earnings swings and the cost plan; a free cash flow recovery that repays floating-rate term loans, with net debt down 8.61% since the fiscal 2025 year end; scale and recurring weekly rental revenue with low customer concentration, which supports debt service through a slow decline; and the absence of a sponsor together with a lender-imposed distribution lock, which keeps cash in the company for now.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, page 59; calculation Q1; calculation F8; calculation L10; calculation E1; calculation F11

The main credit weaknesses are leverage and cover that are thin against falling covenant maximums; revenue erosion from lost customers that shrinks the EBITDA base; a receivables facility that ends within twelve months of the as-of date and must be renewed; a transformation plan that costs more than first stated with unproven savings; and claims outside term debt, namely finance leases, pensions and open litigation, that rank with operating costs and reduce free cash flow.

Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, pages 37, 42; calculation L1; calculation L6; calculation R4; calculation Q3; calculation P1; calculation F4

### Company description

Vestis rents and services uniforms and sells workplace supplies, including restroom and first-aid products, mats, towels and linens, to a very large number of small and large customers in the United States and Canada, with Canada 8.98% of revenue. Weekly route service under multi-year contracts with exit costs gives cash flow visibility, but the business separated from Aramark only in September 2023, so it has a short record as a stand-alone borrower and its historic statements for fiscal 2023 are on a combined basis.
Basis: 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, pages 9, 10, 11, 12, 145; Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation B3
### Ownership and group structure

Ownership is dispersed: the shares were distributed to Aramark stockholders, no sponsor or controlling holder is identified, and a letter agreement with Corvex Management LP and a director is known only by its title. Creditors rely on guarantees and liens from wholly owned domestic material subsidiaries, a bankruptcy-remote entity holds the sold receivables, and whether the Canadian business guarantees the debt is not established because the subsidiary list is not supplied.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, pages 72, 154; 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, page 37
### Revenue drivers and pricing power

Revenue is recurring and weakly cyclical but is being lost account by account. Uniforms revenue fell 7.57% in fiscal 2025 while workplace supplies rose 0.89%, rental revenue fell mainly because lost business exceeded new business, and direct sales fell with the loss of a national account. Net volumes fell 4.5% in the third quarter of 2026 and pricing offset part of it, but pricing power is contested: a shareholder class action alleges misleading statements about pricing practices, so price-led recovery carries legal and retention risk.
Basis: 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, page 68; 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, pages 28, 44; Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation R12; calculation R13; calculation R15
### Cost structure and margin resilience

Cost of services is 73.50% of revenue and selling, general and administrative costs 18.92%, with routes, plants and a largely unionized workforce that make costs quasi-fixed, so a small volume loss costs margin. About 59.23% of employees are union-represented, tariffs and a single-supplier input expose unit cost, and pass-through to customers is limited by contract terms and by retention risk. Margins can be defended only by the plan savings, which the issuer claims are partly realized.

Basis: 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, pages 13, 15, 17, 89; 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, page 4; Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation R16; calculation R17; calculation B1; calculation P4
### Capital intensity and cash flow conversion

The business is capital intensive in fleet, plants and rental merchandise, and reported capital spending was cut 25.91% in fiscal 2025 while new vehicles were financed through finance leases. Cash conversion is therefore best read after lease principal: free cash flow was 44.61% of reported EBITDA over twelve months on that basis, against negative cash flow in fiscal 2025, and working capital released cash in 2026, which will not repeat at the same pace.

Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, page 91; 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, pages 8, 17, 50; EX-99.1_2026-08-11_vstsq3fy26earningsrelease-.htm.jsonl, page 4; calculation R14; calculation F4; calculation F5; calculation F6
### Competitive forces

Rivalry is intense and local: the industry is fragmented, two competitors of size are named, and many customers could run the service in-house. Buyer power is moderate because customers sign multi-year contracts with exit costs but can challenge pricing and contracts, supplier power is concentrated in single-supplier inputs and two plants in Mexico that make about 60% of uniforms and linens, and entry is limited by route density and scale. In-house operation is the main substitute. The result is price pressure that caps margin recovery and increases the importance of retention.
Basis: 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, pages 11–14; Business & governance (CP-1A)
### Macro and policy factors

Three outside factors change credit capacity: tariffs and trade policy on Mexican-made garments, wage and benefit inflation under union contracts and multiemployer plans, and interest rates on floating-rate term loans, where each 1% rise adds about USD 11.4 million a year on the annual report's principal and cuts cover to 2.33x on current figures. Other political and social factors are not a primary credit driver in the documents.
Basis: 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, pages 7, 83; 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, page 4; calculation S1; calculation S2
### Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats

The strengths and weaknesses are those set out above. The opportunities are cross-selling, because customers take about 30% to 40% of the full product line, and the cost plan, which together could lift margin without revenue growth. The threats are further customer loss, tariffs, wage settlements, a ruling in the shareholder litigation, and the distribution lock lifting before leverage reaches 4.50x.
Basis: 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, page 15; 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, page 29; Business & governance (CP-1A)
### Financial profile and credit quality

Scale and diversification are strong, competitive advantage and cost and capex flexibility are average, margin stability and free cash flow stability are weak, liquidity is strong, and refinancing access and financial policy are average. The trend is improving since January 2, 2026, with reported net debt to EBITDA falling from 6.24x to 4.62x, but the constraint is thin cover and the covenant step-downs, and the missing datapoints are the credit agreement, fiscal fourth-quarter results and any peer or market reference.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation L1; calculation L3; calculation L6
### Outlook, tailwinds and headwinds

Over the next 12 to 24 months the issuer guides to fiscal 2026 adjusted EBITDA of USD 310.0 million to USD 315.0 million and free cash flow of USD 160.0 million to USD 170.0 million, with revenue flat to down 2% on a normalized basis. Tailwinds are the plan savings and continued repayment, and headwinds are volume losses, plan costs, the step-down to 4.50x, the lock lifting, and the receivables renewal in August 2027. Beyond fiscal 2027, when the plan is expected to be substantially complete, the documents give no outlook; Term Loan A-2 and the revolver mature in September 2028 and Term Loan B-1 in February 2031, and the sector tailwind of outsourcing is stated only in general terms.
Basis: EX-99.1_2026-08-11_vstsq3fy26earningsrelease-.htm.jsonl, page 4; 10-K_2025-10-03_vsts-20251003.htm.jsonl, pages 10, 67; 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, pages 20, 42; calculation G1
### Downside scenario

The initiating condition is account losses that continue after the targeted volume exits end, with plan savings arriving late. The first operational break is revenue falling faster than costs, so reported EBITDA stalls near its last twelve months level and cash interest, which takes 38.00% of EBITDA, stops falling; free cash flow after finance lease principal, 44.61% of EBITDA, would shrink toward the negative level of fiscal 2025. The financial transmission is leverage that stays near 4.62x while the covenant maximum falls to 4.75x and then 4.50x, with each 1% rise in rates cutting cover to 2.33x.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, pages 20, 44; calculation L1; calculation L14; calculation F4; calculation F5; calculation S2

The liquidity consequence arrives in August 2027: if the receivables facility were not renewed and the sold balance had to be funded on the revolver at July 3, 2026 levels, liquidity would fall by 60.34% and net debt to reported EBITDA would be 5.57x, an illustration that assumes unchanged balances and available revolver capacity. Management levers are capital spending, which was cut 25.91% in fiscal 2025, the distribution lock, asset sales and cost action, so resilience appears sufficient to avoid liquidity distress through fiscal 2027 if the facility is renewed. The observable triggers are listed in the monitoring register.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, pages 20, 37; calculation Q5; calculation Q6; calculation Q7; calculation Q8; calculation R14
### Overall credit view

Overall, Vestis presents an adequate business profile supported by scale, recurring weekly route revenue, low customer concentration and ample undrawn liquidity, but credit quality is constrained by 4.62x leverage, thin cover, falling revenue and claims outside term debt. Cash-flow durability appears adequate because free cash flow has recovered, but part of the recovery is working capital and lease financing. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on renewal of the receivables facility before August 2027 and on leverage staying below the falling covenant maximums. The primary downside path is customer loss with delayed savings. Further analysis would require the credit agreement, fiscal fourth-quarter results and a peer or market reference. The top risk is continued revenue erosion.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-07-03_vsts-20260703.htm.jsonl, pages 20, 37; calculation L1; calculation L6; calculation F4; calculation Q3
